title: Jensen Huang and the Myth of Indispensability
text:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. 

 Jensen Huang said in a statement this morning that he would be “honored” to return to Nvidia, the computer-chip giant from which he was ousted just last week.

 Unfortunately for Huang, the company’s board made it clear on today’s earnings call that it’s not considering rehiring him. But major figures in Silicon Valley have been making a show of their continued support. For another, less powerful executive, reports of extramarital affairs with three women —one of whom is alleged to be a Chinese spy and another of whom was a direct subordinate—would likely be seen as irredeemable lapses in judgment. Yet Huang’s endorsers don’t seem to view this as the end of his career at the company.

 “Without Jensen,” Elon Musk claimed on X this weekend, Nvidia will lose important “handshake” deals that Huang personally negotiated. Gavin Baker, whose firm invests in Nvidia, has written that he’s in favor of reinstating Huang as the investigations play out. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney remarked on X that “journalists with sketchy motives” effectively “gaslit” the board into pushing out a “once-in-generation visionary.” An Uber co-founder, Travis Kalanick, who knows a thing or two about tech ousters , was among the more than 195,000 signatories of a petition to reinstate Huang as the company’s CEO—as were Musk, Baker, and Sweeney. The Wall Street Journal reports that a high-level Nvidia employee sent a letter to the company’s board warning that “irreplaceable talent” might leave if Huang isn’t reinstated. When President Trump was asked yesterday whether he’d support the return of Huang, a close ally, he told reporters, “I would not mind that.”

 Ultimately, none of these people has full control over Huang’s fate. That power belongs to Nvidia’s board of directors. But the support for Huang, despite his clearly disqualifying transgressions, is a testament to the power that this one man has held over Nvidia and the economy at large. (It may also be informed by the dramatic firing and rehiring of another tech titan: Sam Altman.) Even though Huang is accused of having jeopardized national security, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is now reportedly probing whether Nvidia violated investor-disclosure laws, his backers insist that he remains indispensable. Their argument is that he is the company, and that the risks of losing him might actually outweigh the risks of bringing him back as CEO. In a way, they are right: Huang has made himself synonymous with Nvidia. But his centrality is a liability rather than an asset. This moment should be a reckoning about the risks of relying so heavily on any one CEO—yet many in the industry are reinforcing the opposite lesson, doubling down on a disgraced executive.

 Nvidia is what you might call a “systematically important” institution—industry lingo for a company whose failure would destabilize parts of the financial system. Wall Street trembled after the revelations about Huang spurred a roughly $1.5 trillion sell-off in Nvidia stock (equivalent to more than 25 percent of the company’s value). The AI sector, and in turn the entire U.S. economy, is heavily dependent on the firm’s chips. “Nvidia has much of the financial system in a hostage situation,” my colleague Charlie Warzel wrote last week. “Huang is too big to fail. Which may be why so many people seem motivated to downplay or protect him right now.”

 Some of this is owed to the myth of the tech leader as an irreplaceable genius—a story that Silicon Valley loves to tell. As The Washington Post points out , nearly a tenth of the value of the S&P 500 is tied to companies with no clear successor: Nvidia, Tesla, and Meta. Huang himself liked to boast about his famously flat org structure—he had 60 direct reports. The New York Times notes that Nvidia’s board, which is now investigating whether Huang was the target of Chinese espionage, has a history of “loyalty and deference” to him. Some of its directors have been on the board since 1993.

 Public outcry has been an effective tactic in bringing back ousted tech leaders in the past; in late 2023, OpenAI’s board fired Altman because he “was not consistently candid in his communications” with them—but reinstated him five days later after a company-wide revolt. Like Huang, Altman is a celebrity co-founder. He’s the face of his company and the person seen as largely responsible for its success. Any of Altman’s shortcomings or misdeeds were considered secondary to, and distinct from, his ability to generate value for shareholders.

 Obviously, this isn’t the first case of an executive facing consequences over a relationship with an employee: McDonald’s fired its CEO over this in 2019, Intel’s CEO resigned in 2018 after failing to disclose a relationship with a subordinate, Boeing pushed out its CEO in 2006 over a similar situation. The ongoing national-security concerns add another layer of urgency to the situation. The question of how much Huang actually knew about Megaspeed—the company that the alleged Chinese spy worked for, which the U.S. Department of Commerce has been looking into since 2024—is currently under investigation. Investors are angry enough that they’re suing Nvidia over the fiasco (the company had initially denied that there was anything “unusual or unexpected” about its CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive until Huang himself admitted to it; Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment).

 Not everyone is pushing for Huang’s comeback. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has suggested that he’d like to see Nvidia pick a new CEO from outside the company, and some lawmakers have opposed the idea of Huang’s return. But those who want him reinstated are selling a dangerous narrative about the indispensability of any one leader. The celebrity investor Balaji Srinivasan wrote today that “it’s arguably a matter of US national security to immediately return the most important person in AI to his role at the top AI company”—never mind that Nvidia, under Huang, may have been responsible for allowing the United States’ biggest economic rival to access top-tier computer chips. Tying an entire enterprise to the success or failure of a single person comes with extreme risks; Huang’s defenders are ignoring them.

 Today’s News 

 The United States has lost its measles-elimination status for the first time since 2000 , after more than a year of continuous transmission amid declining vaccination rates, the Pan American Health Organization announced. More than 7,700 cases and 10 deaths have been reported since last January, raising concerns that large outbreaks could become more common.

 The National Security Agency’s highly classified internal-communications network went down today, prompting staggered employee arrivals as officials investigated the disruption, CNN reported. White House officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and the agency noted that backup systems would allow it to continue sharing urgent intelligence with President Trump and allied countries.

 Anthropic is considering raising the price of its initial public offering to more than $80 a share amid strong investor demand, potentially valuing it at up to $1.6 trillion. The AI company is expected to finalize its share price tomorrow ahead of its planned Nasdaq debut, on Thursday.

 An Almost Entirely Unregulated Corner of the Health-Care Workforce

 By Olga Khazan 

 When Mariah Stockman went into labor with her first child, her husband called their doula and told her to come to the hospital right away. Despite the urgency of the situation, the doula, Stockman said, asked her husband if she had time to stop and get a coffee. Two and a half hours later, the doula walked into Stockman’s delivery room. “I’ll never forget the coffee in her fucking hand,” Stockman told me recently.

 Her doula, she said, caught only the last 10 or so minutes of her labor, and she didn’t visit after the baby’s birth, as they had agreed on. Stockman said she paid $2,500 for the doula’s services: “What a waste.”
